blocks.text: This vision moves from accusation and cleansing to conditional commission: Joshua stands before the angel, is opposed by the accuser, has his filthy garments removed, and is clothed anew. The closing images introduce the coming servant called the Branch and a stone set before Joshua, described as having seven eyes or facets, alongside the promise that the land’s iniquity will be removed. The exact meaning of these symbolic images remains disputed, so the passage presents them without fully explaining each detail.

The term translated “Satan” can be read as “the accuser” or “the adversary.” A related interpretive tradition notes that, in Job, the Hebrew expression includes an article and can describe a role in the heavenly court rather than an unambiguous personal name for the later devil. Readers may connect the figure in Zechariah with later understandings of Satan, but that connection should be stated as an interpretive development rather than assumed from this scene alone.

The Lord’s rebuke of the accuser is sometimes read alongside a disputed interpretation involving Michael, who declines to issue a slanderous judgment and appeals instead to the Lord’s rebuke. On that reading, Zechariah’s scene does not authorize abusive speech, dramatic exorcism practices, or claims that religious leaders possess unaccountable angelic authority.
